table.brief: A/B test results: Metric / Control (mean, 95% CI) / Variant (mean, 95% CI) / Lift / p-value

conditions.browser: Chromium (Playwright build), macOS system fonts, deviceScaleFactor 1

candidates.name: s1B
candidates.idea: Give metric labels more space while retaining P's intact numerical values. Check whether fewer label wraps improve scanning enough to justify the wider table and a less complete Control group in the initial viewport.
candidates.label: gold

whys: Nearly all metric labels fit on one line, and every interval stays whole, making the full table easy to scan. The first viewport shows only the metric, control mean and part of the control interval, so comparison still requires substantial scrolling.

All intervals and nearly all metric labels stay on one line, giving the table a clear, consistent row rhythm. The initial viewport shows only the metric, control mean and part of the control interval, so comparison requires substantial scrolling.

Nearly all labels and every numeric value occupy one line, producing a compact, orderly table. The first view shows the metric and control mean but only part of the control interval; comparisons require substantial scrolling.

candidates.name: s2B
candidates.idea: Test a fitted alternative that gives more space to numeric columns and less to metric labels. It will still force breaks inside some words and values, but may improve numeric scanning relative to s1C.
candidates.label: bad

whys: The wider metric column improves the labels over D and H, but the numerical columns are so narrow that values and headers break into fragments, making comparison unreliable.

The wider metric column improves label recognition and reduces height, but narrow numeric columns split values, percentages and p-values into fragments. It is the strongest fitting option shown, yet remains hard to use.

The wider metric column improves several labels, but headers and numeric values still break into fragments throughout. The complete grid is visible at once horizontally, yet values are difficult to scan and compare.

candidates.name: d1r0C
candidates.idea: Use a wider scrolling table that keeps confidence intervals and other numerical entries on one line while allowing long metric names to wrap.
candidates.label: gold

whys: Like A, it keeps numerical ranges intact and wraps labels naturally. The extra metric width does not reduce any row heights and leaves less of the control interval visible initially.

Labels wrap at natural boundaries and confidence intervals remain whole. The first viewport shows the metric and control mean, but cuts through the control intervals; several two-line labels make the rows uneven.

Numeric values remain whole and the metric labels wrap naturally. Its first view cuts through several control intervals, while the wider metric column brings no visible reduction in row height compared with C.

candidates.name: d2r1A
candidates.idea: Scrolling alternative: give metric names more room than in B while retaining one-line confidence intervals as in C. This tests whether natural label wrapping can reduce scrolling without breaking statistical values.
candidates.label: gold

whys: Confidence intervals remain whole, and metric labels wrap at natural boundaries. The first viewport cuts through the control interval column, while several two-line labels make the rows uneven.

Natural two-line metric labels and intact intervals make the full table easy to read. Its slightly narrower metric column exposes more of the control interval initially than A, though the variant and results still require scrolling.
Whole numeric values and natural two-line labels support reading. The narrower metric column saves a little scrolling, although the first view still cuts through some control intervals.
The initial view shows the full control group and part of the variant mean. Labels remain recognizable, but several intervals split across lines and some metric labels need three lines.
The narrower table brings the variant mean closer to the initial viewport, but metric labels reach three lines and several confidence intervals split across lines, slowing comparison.
Metric labels remain legible and the first view reaches the variant mean, but several confidence intervals break across lines and three-line labels make the rows tall.

candidates.name: contrast
candidates.idea: Almost equal columns appear orderly on paper but give the long metric labels and confidence intervals far too little room. Words and values would fragment heavily.
candidates.label: bad

whys: The narrow equal columns break labels and numerical values throughout; the slightly wider p-value column does not materially improve the tall, fragmented table.

Like F, this layout fragments nearly every label and many numeric values, creating extremely tall rows. The slightly wider p-value column changes a few breaks but does not materially improve usability.
Like E, this fits the grid at the cost of severely fragmented labels and numbers and very tall rows. The slightly wider p-value column changes little about the overall reading experience.
The first viewport reaches the variant mean, but narrow metric labels take up to four lines, confidence intervals split across lines, and the p-value header wraps.

More columns appear initially, but the narrow metric column produces up to four lines, the p-value header wraps, and time values and intervals break across lines. Those breaks make scanning and comparison laborious.
The first view reaches the variant mean, but the narrow columns split time values and intervals, wrap the p-value heading, and force several labels into three or four lines.
The grid remains intact, but equal narrow columns fragment labels, headers, percentages and p-values into hard-to-read pieces. The very tall rows make comparisons laborious.
Words, numbers and headers fragment throughout; the support metric stretches to twelve lines. The extreme row heights and broken values overwhelm the benefit of seeing every column at once.
The full grid fits, but words, percentages, currency amounts and p-values fragment across many lines. The extremely tall rows make lookup and comparison difficult.

d1.purpose: Report checkout experiment outcomes so readers can assess changes across metrics and judge their uncertainty.
tasks: Find a metric and read its control and variant results.
Compare the two means and confidence intervals within a row.
Scan lift and p-values across metrics to assess the direction, size and statistical evidence of changes.
Read the results sequentially while retaining the metric labels and group headers.
relations: Each mean belongs with its adjacent 95% confidence interval and its control or variant group.
Control and variant values in the same row describe the same metric; lift and p-value summarize the comparison.
A negative lift has different practical implications for completion, abandonment and error metrics.
roles: Metric names are row headers and anchors for lookup.
The two grouped headers distinguish experimental arms; their subheaders identify means and intervals.
Lift and p-value are standalone comparison columns spanning both header rows.
Each body row represents one outcome.
keep_whole: Numbers, signs, percentages, currency amounts and p-values.
Time values and confidence intervals where space permits.
Meaningful metric phrases such as 7-day and 1,000 sessions.
may_wrap: Long confidence intervals at a suitable range separator if the renderer permits it.
Group and subcolumn headers only where necessary.
same_scale: Control and variant mean columns should have similar widths.
Control and variant interval columns should have similar widths.
Lift and p-value columns need comparable room for their short numerical entries.
d1.h_vs_v: A phone-width table forces severe breaks in both labels and numerical values, increasing row height and weakening comparison. Scrolling preserves numerical units and compact rows, at the cost of moving horizontally between metric labels and comparison results.

d2.purpose: Report how a checkout variant performed against a control across conversion, revenue, speed, errors, support demand, and repeat purchase.
tasks: Find a metric and compare its control and variant means.
Read the confidence intervals alongside the means.
Assess the direction and size of the lift and its p-value.
relations: Each mean belongs with the 95% confidence interval immediately to its right.
Control and Variant are parallel groups; lift and p-value summarize their comparison.
Each row must remain easy to trace across all seven columns.
roles: Metric names identify the rows and need enough width to remain recognizable.
The two-tier header groups the paired mean and interval columns.
Lift and p-value are compact comparison columns.
keep_whole: Numbers, percentages, currency amounts, time values, and p-values.
Confidence interval endpoints and their relationship as a range.
Words and hyphenated metric terms where space permits.
may_wrap: Confidence intervals at a natural range boundary when necessary.
same_scale: Control and Variant mean columns should have similar widths.
The two confidence interval columns should have similar widths.
Lift and p-value should have comparable compact widths.
d2.h_vs_v: A viewport-fitting table requires severe splitting of labels and numeric content and will become tall. Scrolling preserves the statistical values and makes rows easier to compare, at the cost of showing fewer columns initially.

d3.purpose: Compare checkout metrics between a control and a variant, including estimated lift and statistical evidence.
tasks: Find a metric and compare its control and variant means.
Read each mean alongside its 95% confidence interval.
Check the direction and magnitude of lift and its p-value.
relations: Control and Variant each group a mean with its confidence interval.
Each row connects a metric to both groups, lift, and p-value.
A negative lift has different practical implications for different metrics.
roles: The first column identifies each metric and anchors row lookup.
The two-level headers organize comparable measurements by experiment group.
Lift and p-value summarize the comparison for each row.
keep_whole: Individual words and hyphenated identifiers where space permits.
Percentages, currency amounts, signed lifts, and p-values.
Confidence interval ranges and time measurements, including their units, where space permits.
The 95% CI header and the p-value header.
may_wrap: Long confidence intervals at a range boundary only if necessary.
same_scale: Control and variant mean columns should be similar in width.
The two confidence interval columns should be similar in width.
Lift and p-value columns should be sized for their short numerical contents.
d3.h_vs_v: A viewport-width table forces severe breaks in labels and numerical values and increases row heights. Scrolling preserves numerical units and comparison structure; allowing metric labels to wrap saves horizontal space while keeping rows reasonably compact.

analysis.strengths: All headers and numerical ranges remain whole, and metric labels wrap at natural word boundaries. The table has a relatively compact height and makes the control and variant columns easy to compare in the full view.
analysis.faults: The first viewport shows the metric and control mean but cuts through the control interval; the variant, lift and p-value require scrolling. Several metric labels occupy two lines.
analysis.spatial_logic: It gives the metric column enough width for mostly short labels and reserves full one-line widths for the confidence intervals, accepting substantial horizontal scrolling.

analysis.strengths: Like P, it keeps headers and numerical ranges whole and uses natural breaks in the metric labels. Its wider metric column provides a little more breathing room.
analysis.faults: The extra 10 px produces no reduction in row height or line count in this render. It also reveals less of the control interval in the first viewport and increases the scrolling distance.
analysis.spatial_logic: It follows P's allocation but gives the row labels a little more space, without a visible payoff for this particular content.

analysis.strengths: It is narrower than P and Q, and the initial viewport reaches the end of the control group. Headers and words remain intact.
analysis.faults: Both monetary and time confidence intervals break across lines, making their endpoints harder to read as ranges. The narrower metric column adds a line to the cart abandonment label, and the table becomes taller.
analysis.spatial_logic: It reduces scrolling by taking width from the metric and both interval columns, trading horizontal space for additional row height and fragmented ranges.

analysis.strengths: All seven columns are present in the viewport without horizontal scrolling, so their overall arrangement is visible at once.
analysis.faults: Headers, words, numbers, percentages and interval endpoints split into fragments. The resulting tall rows and irregular line breaks make lookup and comparison very difficult, despite the absence of scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: It divides the viewport among every column, giving the metric the largest share but leaving too little text width for even short numerical entries.

rounds.insights: The confidence intervals need enough width to keep each range together; their line breaks in R cost more reading effort than the modest reduction in scrolling saves. P uses that space effectively, while Q's extra metric width has no visible benefit. Fitting all seven columns into 360 px forces severe fragmentation, so a fitting design can only be a compromise under the fixed typography and padding.

analysis.strengths: The entire table fits in the viewport, so all columns are present at once.
analysis.faults: Headers, metric names, numbers, confidence intervals and p-values break inside words or values. The resulting tall rows make comparisons difficult and obscure the table's structure.
analysis.spatial_logic: Narrow data columns save horizontal space at the cost of extensive vertical fragmentation. The wider metric column helps, but still splits some labels unnaturally.

analysis.strengths: Headers and numerical values remain intact, and metric labels wrap at natural word boundaries. The compact rows support comparison across the full table.
analysis.faults: The initial viewport cuts through the Control confidence interval and leaves Variant, Lift and p-value out of sight. Readers must scroll to compare the two groups, and row labels may no longer be visible while viewing the rightmost columns.
analysis.spatial_logic: Widths follow content needs: confidence intervals receive more room than means, while the metric column absorbs natural wrapping. This produces a much more readable table, with horizontal travel as the tradeoff.

rounds.insights: The numerical columns cannot remain readable when all seven columns are compressed into 360px. Scrolling preserves values and the grouped header structure, but the position of the first viewport edge matters: showing a complete Control group would make the opening view more coherent.

analysis.strengths: All numeric values and headers remain on one line, and only the longest metric label wraps. The compact rows make it easy to scan and compare results in the full table.
analysis.faults: The initial viewport shows the metric labels and control mean but cuts through the control confidence intervals. The variant and outcome columns require substantial horizontal scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: A generous metric column preserves label continuity, while the confidence interval columns have enough room for their longest values. The resulting width buys a notably compact table.

analysis.strengths: The entire column structure is visible within the viewport, so no horizontal scrolling is needed.
analysis.faults: Headers, metric names, numbers and intervals break inside words and numeric units throughout. The fragmented values are difficult to read or compare, and the table becomes extremely tall.
analysis.spatial_logic: Spreading the available width across seven columns leaves nearly every column too narrow for its contents. The apparent benefit of seeing all columns at once is undermined by the loss of readable values.

analysis.strengths: Headers and numeric values remain intact. The narrower metric column reveals more of the control confidence intervals at first sight and reduces the horizontal scroll distance.
analysis.faults: Several metric labels wrap, making the table substantially taller than s1B. The viewport still cuts through longer confidence intervals, and the variant and outcome columns remain off-screen.
analysis.spatial_logic: Moving 30 px away from the metric column saves horizontal space but creates four two-line data rows. The modest gain in initial visibility comes with a noticeable loss of vertical compactness.

rounds.insights: The numeric columns need considerable width to preserve complete values, especially the two confidence interval columns. A 360 px fit forces destructive breaks across the table; scrolling is much better for reading and comparison. Between the scrolling examples, the metric width has a threshold effect: s1B uses slightly more horizontal space but avoids most of P's extra row height. Neither initial viewport reaches the variant columns.

analysis.strengths: All words and numerical values remain intact in the full table. Grouped headers and comparable measures are easy to follow.
analysis.faults: Three metric labels wrap, making the table taller than necessary. The initial viewport cuts through the control confidence interval and shows none of the variant results.
analysis.spatial_logic: The wide metric column supports row identification, while the confidence interval columns have enough room for their longest values. The remaining widths are closely matched to their contents.

analysis.strengths: All seven columns are present within the viewport, so their overall grouping is visible without scrolling.
analysis.faults: Words, headers, percentages, currency values and p-values break across lines, making lookup and comparison difficult and risking misreading. The extreme row heights disrupt scanning.
analysis.spatial_logic: The available width is divided too thinly across all seven columns; fitting the table transfers the cost into extensive vertical fragmentation.

analysis.strengths: All words and numbers remain intact, with only one metric label wrapping. The compact rows make the full table easy to scan and compare.
analysis.faults: The initial viewport cuts through the control confidence interval and does not show the variant results. The long support metric leaves a single word on its second line.
analysis.spatial_logic: Ten extra pixels in the metric column remove two wrapped labels relative to s2A, substantially reducing height for a small increase in scrolling.

rounds.insights: The scrolling layouts preserve meaningful units and support comparison much better than the fitted example. A small change in the metric width has a large effect on row height near a wrapping threshold. A fitted alternative should prioritize intact metric labels and numeric units, although the available width cannot accommodate all of them.

bad.why: Extremely narrow data columns break headers, numbers and intervals into fragments, producing very tall rows while still requiring horizontal scrolling.
Words and numerical values break across lines throughout, and the table still extends beyond the viewport.
Although it fits, it splits metric names, headers and numerical values into fragments that are difficult to read and compare.

contrast.why: Almost equal columns appear orderly on paper but give the long metric labels and confidence intervals far too little room. Words and values would fragment heavily.

sameFunctionGroups.why: Both hold means for the two test arms; similar widths support comparison, with small differences justified by content.
Both hold confidence intervals and should have comparable room for their similarly sized values.

synthesis.rationale: s1B keeps all numerical values on one line and wraps only one metric label, making lookup and comparison clear after scrolling. s2B is the stronger of the two fitting candidates, with fewer measured internal word breaks and less height than S, but its fragmented headings and values make it unsuitable for publication without further redesign. It is included as the requested fitting-class finalist, not as an endorsement of its readability. P and Q preserve numerical lines with more label wrapping; R reduces scrolling but wraps some intervals.

general: Protect complete numerical values and meaningful text units before optimizing for a narrow viewport.
Give columns with corresponding roles comparable room, adjusted for their actual content.
Judge a scrolling table both as a whole and at its initial viewport.
specific: The two confidence interval columns need substantially more width than the mean columns to keep their longest values on one line.
At 360px, the fixed content and padding leave too little room to keep all seven columns readable without scrolling.

synthesis.tradeoffs: s1B requires substantial horizontal scrolling, and the first viewport shows the metric and control mean but only part of the control interval. R exposes the whole control group initially and is narrower overall, but splits some confidence intervals across lines. Fitting layouts avoid horizontal scrolling at the cost of severe fragmentation and height.
synthesis.uncertain: The best fitting finalist is a relative choice among the supplied candidates; no fitting candidate shown meets a careful publication standard. The preferred scrolling layout also depends on how easily readers can retain the metric label while scrolling to the variant and lift columns.

critique.good: All columns are present in the initial viewport, and the experimental groups remain identifiable in the first header row.
critique.problems: Metric names, headers, numbers, signs and intervals break across lines, making lookup and comparison difficult. The extremely tall rows and uneven wrapping overwhelm the table's structure.
critique.cause: The 100px metric column is narrower than some individual words. The 38–50px numeric columns leave too little room after padding for complete values or headers.

critique.good: Headers and numeric units are legible, paired columns are consistent, and metric names generally wrap naturally. The initial viewport shows the metric and complete control group, with a hint of the variant group.
critique.problems: Several intervals split over two lines, and many rows become tall even where the other values are short. Comparison with variant results, lift and p-values requires scrolling; the viewport cuts through the variant mean.
critique.cause: The 95px interval columns are narrower than the longest complete ranges. The 160px metric column also causes several labels to wrap, while the 644px total width places the variant group beyond the initial viewport.

critique.good: Complete intervals and short values stay on one line, headers are clear, and the wider metric column reduces wrapping. Compact rows and matching group widths make the full table easy to scan.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the control interval, so even the first group's results cannot all be read at once. The greater scroll distance separates labels from the comparison columns, and some labels still wrap despite the extra width.
critique.cause: The 200px metric column and 131–134px interval columns produce a 759px table. Together with the 73px control mean, the metric column pushes much of the control interval beyond the viewport.

critique.good: The entire table fits the viewport, and the metric column gives labels more room than the data columns.
critique.problems: Numbers, signs, headers and intervals break into fragments, making comparisons and even individual values hard to read. The resulting tall rows and uneven density overwhelm the table.
critique.cause: The 39–40 px data columns leave only 18–19 px for text after padding; the 121 px metric column also forces frequent label wrapping.

critique.good: Values and intervals stay whole, headers are clear, and the first viewport shows the complete metric and control columns. The two experiment arms have consistent widths.
critique.problems: Most metric labels occupy two lines, and the support-contacts label occupies three. The variant and comparison columns are initially offscreen, so comparing arms requires scrolling.
critique.cause: The 154 px metric column is narrow for the labels, while the 131–134 px interval columns preserve complete intervals but contribute substantially to the table's width.

critique.good: The table is relatively compact, labels wrap naturally in at most two lines, and numerical units remain intact. The first viewport shows all of the control group and hints at the variant group.
critique.problems: Several intervals split across lines, making their endpoints slower to read and compare. The variant mean is cut by the viewport edge, and lift and p-value require scrolling.
critique.cause: The 95 px interval columns are too narrow for several complete ranges; the 160 px metric column and control columns together place the viewport edge inside the variant mean.

critique.good: The wider metric column improves label scanning and allows several rows to remain on one line. Complete intervals and balanced experiment-arm widths make the full table easy to compare.
critique.problems: The first viewport cuts through the control interval, while the variant and comparison columns are offscreen. Its greater width requires more horizontal travel.
critique.cause: The 200 px metric column and 131–134 px interval columns favor compact rows and whole values at the cost of a 759 px table.

critique.good: The complete table fits in the viewport, and the shaded metric column remains visible alongside every result.
critique.problems: Numbers, signs, percentages, headers and metric words break across lines. The resulting tall, uneven rows make both lookup and comparison difficult.
critique.cause: The 42px result columns leave only about 21px for text; the 107px metric column also forces breaks inside longer words.

critique.good: Labels wrap at sensible boundaries, short numbers remain whole, and the initial viewport contains the metric and the complete control group. The full table has a consistent two-line maximum.
critique.problems: Currency and time intervals split across lines, making their endpoints slower to compare. Variant and comparison results require substantial horizontal scrolling.
critique.cause: The 110px interval columns are narrower than the longest one-line intervals; the 176px metric column and paired result groups make the table 690px wide.

critique.good: The compact scrolling layout keeps words and numeric components whole, with both experimental arms treated consistently. Most of the control group is visible initially.
critique.problems: More percentage intervals wrap than in d1r2B, and the viewport cuts through the variant mean, exposing only fragments of values. The narrower table does not reduce its height.
critique.cause: The 95px interval columns force additional range breaks, while the 160px metric column positions the viewport edge inside the variant mean.

critique.good: All confidence intervals remain on one line, and the wider metric column keeps more labels whole. The shorter rows make the full table easier to scan.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through control intervals, including numbers, and the large horizontal span makes it harder to retain metric context while reaching lift and p-value.
critique.cause: The 200px metric column and 134px and 131px interval columns produce a 759px table; the first interval starts near the viewport edge.

critique.good: All numerical values and confidence intervals remain whole, and the first viewport shows the metric labels and complete control results. The paired groups and standalone comparison columns are clearly organized.
critique.problems: Several metric labels occupy three lines, producing tall rows and large empty areas across the numerical columns. The variant results and comparison columns require scrolling.
critique.cause: The 145px metric column is narrow for labels such as “Cart abandonment rate” and “Time to complete checkout”; the generous 134px and 131px interval columns preserve complete intervals.

critique.good: All seven columns are visible together, and the control and variant columns retain matching widths.
critique.problems: Headers, metric names, numbers, signs and p-values break across lines. The resulting tall, uneven rows make lookup and comparison difficult despite fitting the viewport.
critique.cause: The 80px metric column and 42–52px data columns leave too little space after padding for most labels and numerical units.

critique.good: The first viewport shows complete metric labels and control results. Metric names wrap naturally in at most two lines, and the table is substantially shorter than d1r3A.
critique.problems: Currency and time confidence intervals wrap, making endpoints less immediately comparable. Variant results, lift and p-values remain offscreen initially.
critique.cause: The 176px metric column improves label wrapping, while the two 110px interval columns are too narrow for the longest intervals.

critique.good: The wider metric column gives several labels a single line, while all confidence intervals remain whole. The compact rows and aligned numerical columns support scanning in the full table.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through control confidence intervals, and more horizontal travel is needed to reach the comparison columns. The metric column consumes space without eliminating wrapping for the longest labels.
critique.cause: The 200px metric column combined with the 73px control mean and 134px interval column extends the control group beyond the viewport; the complete table is 759px wide.

critique.good: The labels and headers are readable, the mean columns are compact, and the initial viewport contains the metric and almost the entire control group. Most rows have a consistent two-line rhythm.
critique.problems: The currency and time confidence intervals wrap, making those values harder to compare. Several metric labels also wrap, and variant results and comparison columns require scrolling.
critique.cause: The 121px interval columns are too narrow for the longest ranges. The 165px metric column forces several labels onto two lines.

critique.good: All seven columns are visible at once, so the relationships between groups and comparison columns remain apparent.
critique.problems: Headers, metric names, numbers, signs and percentages break across lines throughout. Tall rows and fragmented values make lookup and comparison extremely difficult.
critique.cause: The 100px metric column and 41–45px data columns provide far less than the space needed for their unbreakable content.

critique.good: The initial view shows the metric and essentially the full control group. The slightly wider metric column gives some labels more natural breaks, while the table is the narrowest scrolling option.
critique.problems: Currency and time intervals wrap, and most metric labels still take two lines. The variant and comparison columns remain off-screen initially.
critique.cause: The 110px interval columns cannot hold the longest ranges, and the 176px metric column is still too narrow for several complete labels.

critique.good: Both groups' intervals stay whole, headers are clear, and more metric labels fit on one line. The shorter rows make scanning the complete table easier.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the control intervals, including several values, and the wider table requires more horizontal travel to reach lift and p-value. The remaining wrapped labels create an uneven row rhythm.
critique.cause: The 200px metric column and 131–134px interval columns preserve content well but push the right edge of the control group beyond the viewport.

critique.good: The entire table is available without horizontal scrolling, and the grouped headers retain their structure.
critique.problems: Labels, headers, numbers, and interval endpoints split across lines, making values difficult to recognize and rows difficult to compare. The resulting height and uneven wrapping overwhelm the table.
critique.cause: The 100px metric column is too narrow for several words, while the 38–49px data columns leave too little space after padding for complete values.

critique.good: Metric labels are recognizable, means and comparison values stay whole, and the parallel groups are easy to distinguish. Its moderate width limits scrolling compared with d2r0C.
critique.problems: Several confidence intervals wrap at the range boundary, increasing row heights and slowing comparison. The initial viewport cuts through the Variant group, so its values and the comparison columns require scrolling.
critique.cause: The 100px interval columns cannot hold the longer ranges on one line. The 160px metric column also wraps many labels, though generally at natural word boundaries.

critique.good: Every label and value stays on one line, producing a calm, compact table with clear row-by-row comparison in the full view.
critique.problems: The initial viewport shows the metric names and only the Control mean; nearly all comparative information is offscreen. The large metric column also makes tracing across the full table more demanding.
critique.cause: The 284px metric column is sized for the longest label, and the 131–134px interval columns are sized for the longest ranges. Together they make the table substantially wider than the viewport.

critique.good: The full table is orderly and compact enough to scan. Values and confidence intervals remain whole, parallel columns are similarly sized, and metric labels wrap naturally.
critique.problems: The initial viewport cuts through the Control confidence intervals, so some values cannot be read without scrolling. Four metric rows are taller than the single-line rows.
critique.cause: The 190px Metric column and 73px Control mean leave only 97px of the 134px interval column visible in the 360px viewport.

critique.good: All seven columns are present in the viewport, and the 120px Metric column gives labels more room than the data columns.
critique.problems: Headers, numbers, ranges and metric words break into fragments. The extreme row heights make both comparison and row tracing difficult; having every column on screen does not make the data readily readable.
critique.cause: The five 38–43px data columns and 44px p-value column leave too little text space after padding. The 120px Metric column also cannot keep some long words whole.

critique.good: The initial viewport shows the complete Control mean and interval, and the narrower table requires less scrolling. Labels and interval endpoints generally remain recognizable.
critique.problems: Several confidence intervals wrap across lines, making their ranges slower to read. The viewport also cuts into the Variant mean, and the repeated two-line rows create a taller table.
critique.cause: The 100px interval columns cannot hold the longest ranges on one line. The 160px Metric column contributes to label wrapping and places the viewport boundary inside the Variant group.

critique.good: Every cell fits on one line, giving the full table a consistent rhythm and making values and ranges easy to scan.
critique.problems: The initial viewport is dominated by labels and shows only the Control mean; the interval and all comparison columns require scrolling. The table is the widest of the candidates.
critique.cause: The 284px Metric column accommodates the longest label on one line but uses most of the 360px viewport.

critique.good: All values and confidence intervals remain whole, the headers are clear, and the initial viewport contains the complete Control group.
critique.problems: The metric column produces mostly two-line labels and a three-line support label, making the table tall. Variant and the comparison columns require scrolling.
critique.cause: The 153px metric column is narrow relative to several labels; the 134px and 131px interval columns preserve ranges but contribute substantially to the scroll width.

critique.good: Labels remain recognizable, the parallel groups are balanced, and no cell exceeds two lines. The complete Control group is visible initially.
critique.problems: Currency intervals wrap at their range boundary, while the time intervals break within the second endpoint, separating seconds from minutes. The resulting rows are harder to scan.
critique.cause: The 110px interval columns cannot hold the longer ranges on one line or keep each time endpoint together.

critique.good: All seven columns are visible at once, and the group structure remains apparent.
critique.problems: Headers, metric words, numbers, units, and p-values fragment across lines. The extreme row heights and broken values make comparisons and lookup difficult.
critique.cause: The 41–45px numeric columns leave only 20–24px for text, and the 100px metric column is too narrow for several words.

critique.good: The paired headers are clear, the mean columns are compact, and metric names wrap without breaking words. The first viewport shows the complete Control group.

critique.good: Both treatment groups are represented near the initial viewport, and the group headings remain recognizable.

critique.good: Complete confidence intervals and compact numeric values make comparisons easy. Most metric labels are recognizable at a glance, and the table is relatively short.

d2r0A.idea: Fit within 359px by giving the metric column the largest share, accepting substantial forced breaks in labels and values.

d2r0B.idea: Use a compact scrolling table with naturally wrapped metric names and moderately wide interval columns to balance row height against horizontal travel.

d2r0C.idea: Use a wide scrolling reference layout that keeps metric names and confidence intervals on one line for fast row scanning.

d1r0A.idea: Fit exactly within 359px, giving the metric column the largest share while accepting severe wrapping or splitting throughout the numeric columns.

d1r0B.idea: Use a moderately wide scrolling table with readable means and comparison columns, allowing metric labels and some confidence intervals to wrap.

d1r0C.idea: Use a wider scrolling table that keeps confidence intervals and other numerical entries on one line while allowing long metric names to wrap.

d3r0A.idea: Fit within 359px, prioritizing the metric column while accepting extensive forced breaks throughout the numerical columns.

d3r0B.idea: Use a moderately scrolling table with naturally wrapped metric labels and full-width numerical values and confidence intervals.

d3r0C.idea: Use a wider scrolling reference table that keeps every metric label and numerical entry on one line.

d2r1A.idea: Scrolling alternative: give metric names more room than in B while retaining one-line confidence intervals as in C. This tests whether natural label wrapping can reduce scrolling without breaking statistical values.

d2r1B.idea: Viewport-fitting alternative: give the metric column more room to preserve recognizable row labels while keeping parallel data columns equal. The severe splitting of numeric values remains an expected cost of fitting all seven columns.

d1r1A.idea: Test a fit-within-359px alternative that protects the longest metric word and gives labels more natural breaks. Numeric values will still fragment severely; this tests whether prioritizing row identification improves the unavoidable phone-width compromise.

d1r1B.idea: Combine B's narrower label area with C's complete confidence intervals. The first viewport should show the metric, control mean and nearly all of the control interval, while preserving intact numerical ranges across the full table.

d3r1A.idea: Test a slightly narrower metric column so the full control group fits within the first viewport. The data widths preserve whole values; inspect whether the narrower labels introduce awkward breaks or excessive row height.

d3r1B.idea: Test a wider metric column to reduce label wrapping while retaining intact numerical values. This trades a wider scrollable table for potentially shorter, easier-to-scan rows.

d3r1C.idea: Test a viewport-width alternative that gives the metric column enough room for its longest unbreakable word. The numerical columns remain severely constrained, so inspect whether the improved labels offer any practical benefit despite fragmented values.

d1r2A.idea: Test a 359 px fitting layout that gives each data column slightly more room while retaining a distinct metric column. Severe breaks are still expected, but this explores whether a more even allocation improves the fitting class.

d1r2B.idea: Test a middle-width scrolling layout: give labels more room than d1r0B and intervals more room than 95 px, while keeping the metric and control columns within the initial 359 px. Check which intervals still wrap and whether the reduced scrolling outweighs those breaks.

d2r2A.idea: Test a scrolling layout whose first 360px contain the complete Metric and Control group. Keep both confidence intervals on one line, accepting additional natural wrapping in metric labels to give the first viewport a useful boundary.

d2r2B.idea: Test a middle-width scrolling layout: give labels more room than d2r0B and intervals more room than its 100px columns, while keeping paired columns equal. Some longer ranges may still wrap, but the table requires less scrolling than d2r1A.

d2r2C.idea: Test a viewport-fitting alternative that gives the numeric columns a little more space than d2r1B. This necessarily sacrifices label width and will still fragment values; it tests whether the distribution improves the fitted class.

d3r2A.idea: Test an intermediate metric width to retain natural label breaks while reducing scrolling relative to d3r1B; keep numerical columns wide enough for complete values.

d3r2B.idea: Test a viewport-fitting compromise that gives confidence intervals more room than d3r1C. It will still break labels and numerical units, so assess it as a separate fitting class.

d2r3A.idea: Test a scrolling compromise: place the end of the Control group at the viewport edge, give metric labels more room than d2r2A, and widen intervals enough to keep time endpoints together while accepting some range wrapping.

d2r3B.idea: Explore a viewport-fitting allocation that gives means and intervals more space at the expense of metric labels, lift, and p-value. It will still split content, but may improve the central Control–Variant comparison; the render will show whether the loss elsewhere is acceptable.

contrast.idea: Almost equal columns appear orderly on paper but give the long metric labels and confidence intervals far too little room. Words and values would fragment heavily.

d2r1A.why: Confidence intervals remain whole, and metric labels wrap at natural boundaries. The first viewport cuts through the control interval column, while several two-line labels make the rows uneven.

d1r0C.why: Like A, it keeps numerical ranges intact and wraps labels naturally. The extra metric width does not reduce any row heights and leaves less of the control interval visible initially.

ref_auto.why: The first viewport reaches the variant mean, but narrow metric labels take up to four lines, confidence intervals split across lines, and the p-value header wraps.

ref_equal.why: The grid remains intact, but equal narrow columns fragment labels, headers, percentages and p-values into hard-to-read pieces. The very tall rows make comparisons laborious.

vc_pref.why: The initial view shows the full control group and part of the variant mean. Labels remain recognizable, but several intervals split across lines and some metric labels need three lines.

s2B.why: The wider metric column improves the labels over D and H, but the numerical columns are so narrow that values and headers break into fragments, making comparison unreliable.

s1B.why: Nearly all metric labels fit on one line, and every interval stays whole, making the full table easy to scan. The first viewport shows only the metric, control mean and part of the control interval, so comparison still requires substantial scrolling.

contrast.why: The narrow equal columns break labels and numerical values throughout; the slightly wider p-value column does not materially improve the tall, fragmented table.

acceptance.unsure: G is the strongest scrolling layout; F is the least difficult of the fitting layouts, though its fragmented numbers still make it a bad table. Correctness scores reflect the visible, intact grid rather than ease of reading broken values.

d1r0C.why: Labels wrap at natural boundaries and confidence intervals remain whole. The first viewport shows the metric and control mean, but cuts through the control intervals; several two-line labels make the rows uneven.

vc_pref.why: The narrower table brings the variant mean closer to the initial viewport, but metric labels reach three lines and several confidence intervals split across lines, slowing comparison.

s1B.why: All intervals and nearly all metric labels stay on one line, giving the table a clear, consistent row rhythm. The initial viewport shows only the metric, control mean and part of the control interval, so comparison requires substantial scrolling.

ref_auto.why: More columns appear initially, but the narrow metric column produces up to four lines, the p-value header wraps, and time values and intervals break across lines. Those breaks make scanning and comparison laborious.

d2r1A.why: Natural two-line metric labels and intact intervals make the full table easy to read. Its slightly narrower metric column exposes more of the control interval initially than A, though the variant and results still require scrolling.

ref_equal.why: Words, numbers and headers fragment throughout; the support metric stretches to twelve lines. The extreme row heights and broken values overwhelm the benefit of seeing every column at once.

s2B.why: The wider metric column improves label recognition and reduces height, but narrow numeric columns split values, percentages and p-values into fragments. It is the strongest fitting option shown, yet remains hard to use.

contrast.why: Like F, this layout fragments nearly every label and many numeric values, creating extremely tall rows. The slightly wider p-value column changes a few breaks but does not materially improve usability.

acceptance.unsure: C is the best scrolling layout; G is the best of the fitting layouts shown, though it is still bad and should not be treated as a publishable fitting solution. The best scrolling choice depends partly on how much weight readers place on initial viewport coverage versus intact values and compact rows.

vc_pref.why: Metric labels remain legible and the first view reaches the variant mean, but several confidence intervals break across lines and three-line labels make the rows tall.

s1B.why: Nearly all labels and every numeric value occupy one line, producing a compact, orderly table. The first view shows the metric and control mean but only part of the control interval; comparisons require substantial scrolling.

d2r1A.why: Whole numeric values and natural two-line labels support reading. The narrower metric column saves a little scrolling, although the first view still cuts through some control intervals.

ref_auto.why: The first view reaches the variant mean, but the narrow columns split time values and intervals, wrap the p-value heading, and force several labels into three or four lines.

ref_equal.why: The full grid fits, but words, percentages, currency amounts and p-values fragment across many lines. The extremely tall rows make lookup and comparison difficult.

d1r0C.why: Numeric values remain whole and the metric labels wrap naturally. Its first view cuts through several control intervals, while the wider metric column brings no visible reduction in row height compared with C.

s2B.why: The wider metric column improves several labels, but headers and numeric values still break into fragments throughout. The complete grid is visible at once horizontally, yet values are difficult to scan and compare.

contrast.why: Like E, this fits the grid at the cost of severely fragmented labels and numbers and very tall rows. The slightly wider p-value column changes little about the overall reading experience.

acceptance.unsure: B is the strongest scrolling layout; its advantage over the narrower A depends on how much the reader values whole intervals and compact rows against seeing more columns initially. G is the strongest fitting layout among those shown, but it is still bad and not a publishable solution.
